title: Gurudongmar Lake and altitude safety
meta_description: Gurudongmar Lake at 5,183 m: the dawn drive from Lachen, altitude sickness signs, who should skip it, how to acclimatise and what to carry in 2026.
summary: Gurudongmar Lake sits at about 5,183 m, 67 km and 3–3.5 hours above Lachen. You reach it only after a night in Lachen, leaving at 4–5 am, and stay about 30 minutes. Sleep at least one night at Lachen first, two if you can, and turn back at Thangu if headache or breathlessness gets worse.

sections.heading: The lake and why it is hard
paras: Gurudongmar is a glacial lake on the high plateau of Mangan district (North Sikkim), about 5 km south of the Tibetan border. Its height is quoted differently: about 5,183 m (17,000 ft) on most travel and road signs, and 5,430 m (17,800 ft) by the Sikkim government, while terrain maps suggest it is a little under 5,150 m. Whichever figure you use, it is higher than Everest Base Camp in Nepal, and you reach it by car in three hours from a village at 2,750 m.

That speed is the problem. Trekkers climb to 5,000 m over ten days. On the Gurudongmar drive you gain about 2,400 m in a morning, from Lachen through Thangu at about 3,900 m to the lake. At the shore the air holds roughly half the oxygen it does at sea level. Most healthy adults manage a short visit well, but some feel very unwell, and a few become seriously ill.

The lake is sacred to Buddhists, who link it with Guru Padmasambhava, and to Sikhs. According to the Wikipedia article on the lake, it stays frozen from about November to mid-May. Please keep it clean and quiet.

sections.heading: Know the warning signs
paras: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) is common above 2,500 m and feels like a bad hangover: headache, nausea, loss of appetite, dizziness, unusual tiredness and poor sleep. Mild AMS often settles with rest, water and no further climbing. On the Gurudongmar day the cure is simple and quick: go down.

Two rarer conditions are emergencies. Fluid on the lungs (HAPE) shows as breathlessness at rest, a wet cough, a rattling chest or blue lips. Fluid on the brain (HACE) shows as confusion, stumbling, slurred speech or extreme drowsiness. Either one means descending immediately and seeing a doctor; the Army and health posts on the route can help. Do not wait to see if it improves.
list: Turn back if a headache gets worse despite rest and water.
Turn back if anyone is breathless while sitting still.
Turn back at once for confusion, unsteady walking or a child who becomes listless.
Tell your driver; they have seen it before and will not argue.

sections.heading: Who should skip the lake
paras: Children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim at all. Beyond that, we advise against Gurudongmar for anyone with heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, asthma or other lung conditions, severe anaemia or sickle cell disease, and for pregnant travellers, unless their own doctor has cleared a short visit to 5,000 m. Anyone who had AMS badly on a past trip should think twice.

Many families split the group: the fit adults go to the lake while children, seniors and anyone feeling poorly stay at Lachen or wait at Thangu. That is a sensible choice, not a lost day. Yumthang above Lachung, at 3,564 m, gives the same high-valley feeling at a far kinder height. Foreign nationals cannot visit Gurudongmar in any case.

sections.heading: How to acclimatise properly
paras: Never attempt Gurudongmar on the day you drive up from Gangtok. It is not permitted and it is not safe. The minimum is one night at Lachen, and the better plan is two: arrive, rest a full day with a short walk to Lachen Monastery, and go to the lake on the third morning. That is why we build most Gurudongmar trips as 3N/4D or longer, with two nights in Lachen.

A night or two in Gangtok (1,650 m) before going north also helps, as does a gentle start in Dzongu (about 700–1,500 m). Drink 3 to 4 litres of water a day, skip alcohol and smoking up north, eat light carbohydrate meals, and walk slowly. Some travellers take acetazolamide to help acclimatisation; it is a prescription medicine with side effects, so ask your own doctor before the trip rather than borrowing tablets on the road.

sections.heading: Three ways to build the trip
paras: How you schedule the nights matters more than any pill or oxygen can. These are the three shapes we use, from the hardest to the gentlest.

The 2-night loop: Gangtok to Lachen on day one, Gurudongmar at dawn on day two, then down and across to Lachung for the night, Yumthang on day three and back to Gangtok. It works for fit young adults who have already spent a night or two in Gangtok, but day two is long and you reach the lake after a single night at 2,750 m.

The 3-night loop: two nights in Lachen, one in Lachung. Either you go to the lake on the first morning and rest on the afternoon of day two, or, better, you spend the second day walking around Lachen and go to the lake on day three. This is the plan we suggest for most travellers, including healthy seniors.

The slow plan: a night in Dzongu at about 1,200 m on the way up, then two nights in Lachen, then Lachung. Three steps up instead of one jump. It suits families with older children, first-time Himalaya travellers and anyone who has felt the altitude before. It also gives a fall-back if the Lachen road closes: you still have Dzongu and Lachung.

sections.heading: What to carry on the day
list: Warm layers: thermal inner, fleece, down or padded jacket, windproof shell, woollen cap, gloves. It is often −5 to −15 °C at dawn.
Sunglasses with UV protection and sunscreen; the light off snow and water is harsh.
A refillable bottle with warm water, and dry snacks such as biscuits, nuts and chocolate.
Your ID and permit copy in a pocket for the check posts.
A small portable oxygen can is often sold in Lachen; it is a comfort, not a treatment, and does not replace going down.
Your regular medicines, a strip of paracetamol, and any prescription your doctor gave you for altitude.

sections.heading: At the shore
paras: Walk, do not run. Climbing the few steps to the viewpoint feels like a long staircase at this height. Keep the visit to 20 to 30 minutes, take your photos, and then go down. Avoid lying on the ground or napping in the car at the lake. Do not throw coins, scarves or plastic into the water. Check current road and permit status before you travel, since the Lachen road reopened only in September 2026 after a long closure.

On the way down, stop at Thangu or the Chopta Valley area only if everyone feels well, and keep the stop short. Most people feel better within an hour of leaving the lake. If anyone still has a strong headache or breathlessness back in Lachen, do not cross to Lachung that afternoon: rest, drink water, and see the health centre in Lachen or Chungthang. Tell us, and we will rework the rest of the trip.

faqs.a: Most road and travel signs give about 5,183 m (17,000 ft). The Sikkim government quotes 5,430 m (17,800 ft), and terrain maps suggest a little under 5,150 m. Whichever figure is right, it is one of the highest lakes in India reachable by car, and the oxygen at the shore is roughly half of sea level.

faqs.q: Can I visit Gurudongmar Lake from Gangtok in one day?
faqs.a: No. A same-day trip from Gangtok is not permitted and is unsafe, because you would climb from 1,650 m to over 5,000 m in a few hours. You must spend at least one night in Lachen, leaving for the lake at about 4–5 am. We recommend two nights in Lachen for better acclimatisation.

faqs.q: Is Gurudongmar safe for senior citizens?
faqs.a: For healthy seniors who have been cleared by their doctor, a short visit after two nights in Lachen is usually manageable. For anyone with heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure or lung conditions, we advise against it. Many seniors choose to wait at Thangu or Lachen while the rest of the group goes, which is a sensible choice.

faqs.q: How long can you stay at Gurudongmar Lake?
faqs.a: Plan on 20 to 30 minutes at the shore. The drive takes 3 to 3.5 hours each way, and staying longer at 5,000 m raises the risk of altitude sickness without adding much. The Army also expects vehicles to head back by late morning, because weather on the plateau worsens after midday.

faqs.q: What are the signs of altitude sickness at Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Headache, nausea, dizziness, unusual tiredness and loss of appetite are the common signs of mild altitude sickness. Breathlessness at rest, a wet cough, confusion, stumbling or extreme drowsiness are emergencies that need immediate descent and a doctor. On this day trip the best treatment is simple: go back down towards Thangu and Lachen.

faqs.q: Should I carry oxygen to Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: A small portable oxygen can, sold in Lachen and Gangtok, can make a few minutes more comfortable, and many drivers carry one. It is not a treatment for altitude sickness and does not replace descending. Proper acclimatisation, a night or two in Lachen, water and a slow pace matter far more.

The lake is usually frozen from about November to mid-May, according to the Wikipedia article on the lake. A part near one shore is said to stay unfrozen, which local Buddhists link to Guru Padmasambhava. Heavy snow can close the road beyond Thangu between December and March, so winter visits are never certain.

No. Gurudongmar Lake is not open to foreign nationals, because it lies close to the border. Foreign groups of two or more can visit Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point with a Protected Area Permit. Access to Lachen and Thangu for foreigners has been unclear in 2026, so ask us before planning.

faqs.q: Can children go to Gurudongmar Lake?
faqs.a: Children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim at all. Older children can visit with a permit, but children show altitude sickness less clearly than adults, often as crankiness, vomiting or listlessness. If you take children, keep the visit short, watch them closely and turn back at the first sign of trouble.
